analysis.one_liner: Blocked OSHA from issuing workplace ergonomics rules until a National Academy of Sciences study was done.
analysis.headline: Backed by 48 senators, the bill was referred to the Senate labor committee and never received a hearing or vote before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: In 1999 the Labor Department's safety agency, OSHA, was preparing the first federal ergonomics standard — rules designed to reduce repetitive-stress injuries among workers who lift, type, scan, or assemble all day. This bill would have legally barred OSHA from proposing or finalizing any such rule until the National Academy of Sciences finished a peer-reviewed study on whether repetitive work actually causes those injuries, plus 30 more days. Employers in repetitive-task industries would have avoided the standard's compliance costs for as long as the delay lasted; workers with injury risk would have waited.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries were employers in industries with heavy repetitive work — manufacturing, meatpacking, retail, food service, and data-entry-heavy offices — who faced billions of dollars in compliance costs under OSHA's pending ergonomics rule. Delaying the rule meant those costs, plus the risk of an unfavorable final standard, would be put off indefinitely pending a study whose timing Congress itself had mandated.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibited the Secretary of Labor, through OSHA, from proposing or issuing any ergonomics standard, regulation, or guideline until the National Academy of Sciences completed a peer-reviewed study on the link between repetitive workplace tasks and musculoskeletal disorders and reported to Congress, plus a 30-day waiting period.

The bill's stated rationale was that basic questions about the diagnosis and causes of musculoskeletal disorders were disputed, that a 1998 National Academy of Sciences workshop and a 1997 federal safety research report showed insufficient evidence to assess worker risk from repetitive motions, and that it was therefore premature for OSHA to regulate.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, workers exposed to repetitive strain — assembly line workers, meat and poultry processors, grocery cashiers, nurses and aides lifting patients, and office workers — would have continued to develop carpal tunnel syndrome, back injuries, and similar conditions without the engineering controls, training, and medical management an ergonomics standard would have required, with the costs falling on the injured workers and their families.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers at risk of repetitive-stress injuries

drawbacks.text: A delay in an ergonomics standard meant workers in high-risk jobs would keep getting injured while the study ran; the bill gave OSHA no authority to act on interim evidence even where employers already used accepted ergonomic fixes voluntarily.

Supporters would honestly acknowledge the tension: Congress had already agreed in 1998 to fund the National Academy study, but this bill converted a study into a hard legal barrier, so if the study ran long or its report was contested, workers would have no federal protection at all for an open-ended period.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated goal — grounding a sweeping workplace rule in completed, peer-reviewed science — is a legitimate one, and the science on how much repetitive motion alone causes these injuries was genuinely contested at the time. But the bill's real-world effect was one-directional: it imposed a legal freeze that only employers gained from and only exposed workers paid for, and it set no deadline for the study, so the delay could have lasted indefinitely. On balance it was a delay vehicle rather than a balanced design.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, and the Congress ended in January 2001 with no vote ever taken.

narrative.text: Senator Christopher Bond introduced the SENSE Act on May 18, 1999, with 29 original cosponsors including the majority and majority-whip leadership of the Senate.
The bill was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
It ultimately drew 48 cosponsors — 47 Republicans and 1 Independent — but the action record shows no committee hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred.
The 106th Congress ended January 3, 2001, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, nothing blocked OSHA from acting, and the agency went on to issue a federal ergonomics standard in late 2000 — so the short-term winners were OSHA and the workers the standard was designed to protect, while the employer groups that had backed the delay lost their vehicle. (The incoming administration and Congress repealed that standard in 2001 by a separate process, which this bill played no part in.)

for.name: Sen. Christopher S. Bond
for.role: U.S. Senator from Missouri; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the SENSE Act and led its sponsorship.

for.name: 47 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the Senate Majority Leader and Majority Whip.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred on May 18, 1999; no further action appears in the record.

against.name: President Bill Clinton
against.what_they_did: His administration pressed forward with OSHA's ergonomics rulemaking rather than agreeing to delay legislation, and OSHA issued the final standard in November 2000.

sides.party_line_note: All 48 cosponsors were Republicans or aligned Independents, and no Senate Democrat appears among them; the bill's failure was inaction rather than a recorded split, since it never reached a vote.

industries.industry: Repetitive-task employers (manufacturers, meat and poultry processors, retailers, food service, offices)
industries.note: The bill would have frozen the ergonomics rulemaking that would have required these employers to redesign workstations, rotate tasks, and manage injury reporting, avoiding what were projected to be very large compliance costs. The savings came directly out of injury protections for their own workforces, so their interest ran against the workers exposed to repetitive strain.

Unions had sought a federal ergonomics standard for years as a way to cut musculoskeletal injuries; the bill would have pushed that standard behind an open-ended study, costing their members protection.
